issues.legal_issue: A substantial question of law arises in a second appeal when lower courts materially misread or misinterpret title documents and related evidence bearing on identification of the property and the parties’ rights.
material_facts: The claim to the disputed land rested on an old deed of sale and related documentary descriptions and a plan.
The descriptions and boundaries in the deed and other documents did not readily correspond with the plan and the claimed location of lanes and neighbouring properties.
The lower courts’ treatment of the documents and plan was challenged as involving misreading and misinterpretation, and the High Court allowed the cross-objection after formulating questions of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to consider the matter as involving a substantial question of law; the challenge to that conclusion had no merit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a High Court generally does not disturb concurrent findings of fact, but may do so where material evidence has been ignored or misread, or findings rest on an erroneous legal approach. Under Hero Vinoth v. Seshammal, construction of a document involving a legal principle, and a material legal question affecting the parties’ rights, may raise a substantial question of law. Rev. Fr. M.S. Poulose v. Varghese recognizes that interpretation of document recitals may involve such a question. Commission of Customs (Preventive) v. Vijay Dasharath Patel also recognizes that ignoring material facts or misreading evidence may warrant High Court consideration.

predicates.second_appeal_review: The case is a second appeal in which review is limited to substantial questions of law.
predicates.title_documents_bear_on_rights: A party relies on title documents whose interpretation bears on the parties’ rights to the property.
predicates.property_identification_evidence_is_mate: Documents or a plan are relied on to identify the property at issue.
predicates.lower_court_misread_or_misinterpreted_ma: The lower court misread or misinterpreted evidence material to the property claim.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns material title and identification evidence that the lower court misread or misinterpreted, a substantial question of law arises.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking possession must identify the property claimed sufficiently for the court to determine what was purchased and for possession to be delivered under any decree.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought relief concerning land claimed under a deed of sale.
The deed, later documents and a plan contained descriptions of boundaries, lanes and neighbouring properties that did not readily correspond.
The plaintiffs relied on a sketch to establish the location and identity of the land.
issues.conclusion: The property had to be adequately identifiable, and the plaintiffs had to show that the property described in their deed corresponded with the property identified by the other evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A plaintiff seeking recovery of possession must establish the cause of action concerning the property and identify it sufficiently for the court to determine the subject of the claim and for the executing court to deliver possession. The court applied this requirement to the deed and identification evidence in the case.

predicates.possession_claim: A plaintiff seeks recovery of possession of property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_title_document: The plaintiff relies on a document to establish what property was acquired.
predicates.identification_evidence_does_not_readily: The descriptions in the title document and the other evidence relied on to locate the property do not readily correspond.

issues.definition: In a possession claim relying on a title document, a mismatch between that document’s description and the identification evidence means the property must still be identified sufficiently for a possession decree.

issues.legal_issue: A court will not determine whether an appeal or cross-objection abated when the question was not raised before the High Court and deciding it would require resolution of disputed facts.
material_facts: A party argued that a cross-objection had abated after a cross-objector died during the second appeal and that legal representatives had not been brought on record within the prescribed period.
The opposing party contended that the deceased cross-objector’s estate was substantially represented by other parties already on record.
The abatement question had not been raised before the High Court or in the appeal memorandum, and the Supreme Court considered substantial representation to be a disputed factual question.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not decide whether the cross-objection had abated and declined to resolve the disputed question of substantial representation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 22 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal abates automatically if the deceased party’s legal representatives are not brought on record within the prescribed period, though abatement may be set aside on an appropriate application. Mithailal Dalsangar Singh v. Annabai Devram Kini states that abatement provisions should be construed strictly and applications to set aside abatement considered liberally. The Court declined to determine the case-specific question because it had not been raised earlier and depended on disputed facts.

predicates.appeal_or_cross_objection: The proceeding before the court is an appeal or cross-objection.
predicates.abatement_question_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the abatement question before the High Court or in the appeal memorandum.
predicates.representation_of_deceased_estate_is_dis: The parties dispute whether the deceased party’s estate is substantially represented by those already on record.

issues.definition: When an abatement question in an appeal or cross-objection was not raised below and representation of the deceased party’s estate is disputed, the court does not adjudicate that question.
